questions.q: State the three journal entries required at the end of each accounting year when depreciation is charged directly to the asset account.
questions.a: The three entries are: (1) Depreciation A/c Dr. → Asset A/c (for charging depreciation to asset), (2) Profit & Loss A/c Dr. → Depreciation A/c (for transferring depreciation to P&L). The purchase entry (Asset A/c Dr. → Bank/Vendor) occurs only in the year of purchase. A wrong answer listing four entries or reversing the debit/credit reveals confusion between the two recording methods or misunderstanding that depreciation is a non-cash expense.

questions.q: Explain why the Asset Account shows a decreasing balance each year under this method, and how this differs from the Provision for Depreciation method in terms of Balance Sheet presentation.
questions.a: Under this method, depreciation is credited directly to the Asset Account, so its carrying amount reduces annually. The Balance Sheet shows the asset at net book value (cost minus accumulated depreciation). In the Provision method, the Asset Account remains at original cost, and accumulated depreciation appears separately as a deduction on the asset side or on the liabilities side. A student who says "both methods show asset at original cost" confuses the two methods and misses the fundamental distinction in ledger structure.

questions.q: A machine costing ₹2,00,000 is purchased on 1st April 2023. Depreciation is charged at 10% p.a. on straight line basis. Books close on 31st March. Pass journal entries for the first two years and show the Machine Account for both years.
questions.a: Year 1 (2023-24): Depreciation = ₹20,000. Entries: (1) Depreciation A/c Dr. 20,000 → Machine A/c 20,000; (2) P&L A/c Dr. 20,000 → Depreciation A/c 20,000. Machine A/c: Dr. Bank 2,00,000 | Cr. Depreciation 20,000, Balance c/d 1,80,000. Year 2 (2024-25): Same entries. Machine A/c: Dr. Balance b/d 1,80,000 | Cr. Depreciation 20,000, Balance c/d 1,60,000. A wrong answer using reducing balance or showing accumulated depreciation in a separate account indicates failure to apply the straight line calculation and the "charge to asset" method simultaneously.

questions.q: Compare the total charge to Profit & Loss Account over the asset's life under this method versus the Provision method. Does the method of recording affect the total depreciation expense recognised?
questions.a: No, the total depreciation expense charged to P&L over the asset's useful life is identical under both methods because both follow the same depreciation calculation (SLM or WDV). The recording method only affects ledger structure and Balance Sheet presentation, not the expense amount. A student who claims one method results in higher total depreciation confuses accounting policy (method of calculation) with recording technique (ledger presentation).

questions.q: Critique this statement: "Charging depreciation to the asset account violates the historical cost principle because the asset no longer appears at its original cost."
questions.a: The statement is incorrect. Historical cost principle requires recording the asset initially at its acquisition cost, which is done. Subsequent depreciation reflects allocation of that cost over useful life — not a revaluation. The net book value (cost less accumulated depreciation) is the correct carrying amount per accounting standards. A student agreeing with the statement misunderstands that historical cost applies to initial recognition, not permanent display at original cost regardless of consumption.

questions.q: Design a transaction scenario where a business purchases an asset mid-year, incurs installation costs, and uses the straight line method with charging to asset account. Specify all data needed for a classmate to prepare the full ledger for Year 1 and Year 2.
questions.a: A good scenario includes: purchase date (e.g., 1st Oct 2023), purchase price (e.g., ₹4,00,000), installation cost (e.g., ₹50,000), estimated useful life (e.g., 5 years), residual value (e.g., ₹50,000), accounting year-end (31st March), depreciation method (SLM). The classmate must calculate Year 1 depreciation for 6 months on total cost (₹4,50,000 - ₹50,000) × 10% × 6/12 = ₹20,000, Year 2 full year ₹40,000. A poor scenario omits installation cost, residual value, or mid-year purchase, making the problem unsolvable or ambiguous.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Charging depreciation to the asset account is a method of recording depreciation where the depreciation amount for each period is directly credited to the fixed asset account, reducing its book value, and debited to the Depreciation Account which is ______ closed by transferring to the Profit and Loss Account.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you buy a ______ for ₹60,000 for your freelance graphic design work.
What is Charging depreciation to the asset account? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Charging depreciation to the asset account is a method of recording depreciation where the depreciation amount for each period is directly credited to the fixed asset account, reducing its book value, and debited to the Depreciation Account which is subsequently closed by transferring to the Profit and Loss Account.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Charging depreciation to the asset account?
questions.a: Students often believe that crediting the Asset Account for depreciation means the business is "receiving money" or that the asset's market value is being adjusted.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to independently pass journal entries for asset purchase, depreciation charge, and transfer to Profit & Loss Account under this method, prepare the Asset Account and Depreciation Account ledger for 3+ years with correct balancing figures, and show the correct Balance Sheet presentation at net book value.
